# What the Eel Knows

There is a fact I have trouble holding in my head, and I'd like to hand it to you while it's fresh: no human being has ever seen two eels mate.

Sit with that a moment. We have filmed giant squid in the abyss and snow leopards in the Himalaya. We have landed a robot on a comet and watched, in real time, a whale deliver a calf. We can sequence the genome of anything that holds still, and of plenty of things that don't. And yet the European eel, an animal so ordinary that it turns up in garden ponds and drainage ditches and buckets outside bait shops, has never once, in the entire history of human observation, been caught in the act of reproduction. Not in the wild. Not in an aquarium, where eels have been kept for more than a century and have refused, always, to spawn the natural way. The most ordinary act of its existence has been performed, by now, some unimaginable trillions of times, and witnessed by no one.

For most of history this was not a charming curiosity. It was an embarrassment. Every other animal has parents. Chickens come from eggs laid by chickens. Mayflies hatch from rivers in which you can find their larvae. The eel, by contrast, simply appeared, each spring, in rivers across Europe, with no visible origin and no visible means of production. It arrived after heavy rains, sometimes crossing wet meadows on damp nights, nosing over grass and stone as if it were condensing out of the dew itself. Medieval naturalists weren't sure whether it was a fish or a serpent, and some declined to eat it on the grounds that its origins were, in the strictest sense, unknowable.

The eel has been getting away with this for as long as there have been people to notice.

What we actually know about the eel's life reads less like biology than like a cold case file, assembled from circumstantial evidence over thousands of years. Here is the reconstruction, as best we can make it: European eels are born, presumably, in a region of open ocean called the Sargasso Sea, a shoreless stretch of warm water east of Bermuda. From there, the newborn larvae drift for one to three years across the entire Atlantic, riding the Gulf Stream, until they arrive at the coasts of Europe as glass eels, creatures the size of a fingernail and about as transparent. They darken, wriggle upstream, and spend the next ten, twenty, forty years in freshwater as yellow eels. Then, when some interior clock strikes, they transform again: they turn silver, their eyes enlarge, their digestive tracts begin to dissolve, and they stop eating entirely. Swimming on stored fat alone, they travel five thousand kilometers or more back to the Sargasso, spawn once, and presumably die.

This means that every European eel you have ever seen crossed an ocean as an infant. The one in your garden pond. The ones in the Seine, the Thames, the Danube. It is as if someone told you, with a straight face, that every sparrow in London hatched in the middle of the Pacific.

For a long time, nobody bought it. Aristotle examined the question and concluded, reasonably enough given what he could see, that eels sprang spontaneously from the mud of riverbeds, generated from what he called the entrails of the earth, with neither egg nor copulation involved. Pliny the Elder offered that adult eels reproduce by scraping themselves against rocks, the scrapings coming alive. Folk tradition across Europe held that eels were born of horsehairs fallen into water, a belief so persistent that it took actual science to untangle it: certain hairworms really do seem to materialize from horse troughs, having completed their strange lives inside insects, and the confusion was almost forgivable. The eel's problem was that it offered no evidence of anything. A freshwater eel has no visible gonads. It is, for most of its life, effectively prepubescent, a creature whose sexuality is deferred until the journey it takes in secret, at the end of which it is beyond our reach. It outlasted every theory about itself by simply declining to be caught at it.

Which brings us, improbably, to Sigmund Freud.

In 1876, Freud was a nineteen-year-old medical student in Vienna, and his professor assigned him a research trip to Trieste with a specific mission: dissect eels and find the testes. This was, at the time, a genuine open question of comparative anatomy. Freud spent roughly four months at the zoological station, working through some four hundred eels, knife in hand, looking for the answer to where eels come from. He found, in a few specimens, tissue he took to be immature sexual organs, published a small, cautious paper, and admitted that the material at hand could not settle the matter. The mature male eel eluded him; eels mature only on that secret journey he could not follow. He left Trieste, left the eels, and went on to a career built on the conviction that nothing hidden stays hidden forever, that every symptom has a source, that if you dig deeply enough you will find the organ of the matter. The first great mystery he failed to solve was, fittingly, sex. One imagines four hundred eels, each one interrogated at length, each one refusing to say a word.

The eel's baby had been hiding in plain sight for a century before anyone connected the dots. Naturalists had long known of a creature called the leptocephalus: a flat, transparent thing shaped like a willow leaf, so clear you could see straight through its body, which moved through the sea with a strange sideways flutter. It was described and named in the eighteenth century as its own genus, its own species, its own kind of animal, because it looked nothing whatsoever like an eel. Only in the 1890s, when two Italian zoologists raised the larvae through metamorphosis in tanks at Messina, was it established beyond doubt that the leaf was the child. The eel does not merely grow up. It becomes, over its life, several different animals wearing one another's skin.

The man who finally cornered the secret was a Dane named Johannes Schmidt, and he went at the problem like a detective reconstructing a crime from scuff marks. His logic was elegant: larval eels grow as they drift, so if you catch them everywhere in the ocean and measure them, the smallest ones, the youngest ones, will point you toward the cradle. From 1904 onward, funded in part by Danish beer money through the Carlsberg Foundation, Schmidt trawled the Atlantic with fine-mesh nets, for nearly two decades, pausing for the First World War, counting and measuring larvae by the thousand. The map converged slowly, like a shy witness eventually pointing west, then southwest. In the early 1920s he could announce it: the smallest larvae, just a few millimeters long, came from the Sargasso Sea, that vast, uncanny region bounded not by land but by currents, carpeted with drifting sargassum weed, sitting in the windless horse latitudes that old sailors associated with becalmed ships and rotting crews. The spawning ground of every eel in every European river turned out to be closer to New York than to Lisbon.

Even now, with Schmidt's map a century old, the strangeness has not worn off, and the case is not closed. No one has ever observed eels spawning in the Sargasso or anywhere else. No one has ever collected a fertilized European eel egg from the open sea; the smallest larvae are the earliest evidence anyone has found. For decades, not a single adult eel was ever caught in the open Atlantic mid-journey. Only in recent years have satellite tags followed migrating eels into Sargasso waters, and even then the tags mostly surfaced on their own, reporting positions after the fact. What data we have suggest the eels spend their days diving to depths of several hundred meters and rising again at night, for reasons nobody understands. In captivity, researchers have coaxed eels to spawn only through hormone injections, and the larvae rarely survive more than a few days. The life cycle has never been closed. Which means that every farmed eel on Earth, in every aquaculture facility from Japan to Madagascar, began as a wild-caught baby. We can grow eels, but we cannot make them. The last open question of eel biology happens to be the choke point of eel conservation, and nobody planned it that way.

The eel, meanwhile, plays by its own rules, and the rules are strange. Its sex is not fixed at conception but negotiated with its circumstances: crowded waters produce males, spacious waters produce females, as if the eel were checking the neighborhood before deciding what to be. Its puberty can be postponed for decades. There was, until 2014, an eel in a well in the village of Brantevik, in southern Sweden, reportedly thrown into the well as a glass eel in 1859, that lived to be about a hundred and fifty-five years old, outlasting the American Civil War, two world wars, and several successive generations of the family that kept it. Wells full of eels were once a working tradition across northern Europe: a living larder in the backyard, and, if the stories are to be believed, something like a companion. In Māori tradition, the great longfin eels are taonga, treasures; some were regarded as guardians of specific places, beings you did not simply catch but negotiated with. An animal that breathes through its skin, climbs damp stone, and crosses dewy meadows at night makes a better neighbor than a fish.

Which is what makes the last chapter so hard to write. Since the late 1970s, the number of glass eels arriving in Europe has fallen by something like ninety to ninety-five percent. The European eel is listed as critically endangered. The causes appear to be stacked, a casino of bad luck: dams and hydroelectric turbines that kill migrants in both directions, habitat loss, pollution, shifting currents in the spawning grounds themselves, and a parasitic worm from East Asia that hitchhiked in imported eels in the 1980s and now inflames their swim bladders, possibly ruining their buoyancy for exactly the crossing their lives are built around. We may have broken their road home before we ever knew where home was.

And then there is the market. Baby eels are called white gold for a reason; at their peak they have sold for over a thousand euros a kilogram, flown live to Asia to stock farms, smuggled by the ton in luggage and shipping containers in a black market that Europol pursues across borders. In the Basque Country, a plate of true elvers has become so expensive that restaurants serve gulas, a counterfeit made of surimi pressed into the shape of baby eels. Spain now eats an imitation of a mystery.

There is something almost tender in the countermeasures. In New Zealand and Sweden, conservationists net migrating adult eels at dams and drive them, by truck, around the turbines to the sea. Human beings ferrying eels to their weddings because we paved over the road they would have walked.

Rachel Carson understood the shape of this story early. Her first book opens by following a silver eel named Anguilla out of her coastal pool, down the river, and across the Atlantic toward the Sargasso, and you can feel in it the recognition that the eel's life is fundamentally a homecoming, a return to a place it has never seen. I think about the eel more than is probably reasonable, and what stays with me is this: it kept its secret through Aristotle and the fall of Rome, through Freud's four hundred scalpels and Schmidt's twenty years of trawling. It survived every theory ever written about it. And now the secret risks being retired unopened, not solved but orphaned, its only keeper slipping away.

Every other animal eventually told us where babies come from. The eel is the last holdout, the sole confidant of its own origin, and I find I want that secret to survive even unconfessed. Somewhere tonight, a glass eel smaller than a thumbnail is nosing up a dark river, transparent enough to see the stones through, carrying somewhere in its body the answer to a question humans have been asking for two and a half thousand years. I hope it makes it. I hope nobody ever needs a scan to know what's inside it. Some things should stay one step ahead of us. But mostly I hope it makes it because the answer only matters if someone is left alive to ask.

The larva was first described in 1783 or so as "Leptocephalus" — a distinct animal. This is a nice beat: the baby eel was, for over a century, classified as its own species because it looks nothing like an eel.

6. Johannes Schmidt, the Danish oceanographer: From about 1904 (with breaks — WWI) into the 1920s, he trawled the Atlantic with fine mesh nets, counting and measuring larval eels. His paper "The Breeding Places of the Eel" (1923). The Sargasso — bounded not by land but by currents, the calm horse latitudes, carpeted in sargassum weed, nicknamed the "Sea of Lost Ships" in sailor lore, home of the Bermuda Triangle mythology. The thought that all European eels are born in a sea without shores, roughly two million square miles of open ocean east of Bermuda.
